title: Feedback wanted on pyorder, a Python definition-ordering linter
author: Winipedia

text:
Any reason this is a standalone tool rather than a custom rule in an existing linter/formatter? esp since it’s written in Python.

How should caller-before-callee behave when there are cycles or definition-time dependencies?

Falling back to source order seems reasonable here

Would you trust an auto-fix that moves definitions while preserving their source text?

I would trust it more than one that doesn’t preserve the source text
author: yangdanny97

text:
I could see this being useful. Function ordering can get really messy.
I usually put Classes at the top, and dataclasses at the very top. I cannot see myself changing that habit, even for the sake of a useful linter.
It’s not obvious to me whether callers belong above or below callees. But being predictable there is a nice feature.
When there is a cycle, it would make sense to me to treat that cycle as a block, sort within that cycle following the normal rules (alphabetically if there are no other determining factors), and determine the position of the block by looking at the top element of the block.
I think there are significant problems using this in the way I usually use a linter (as something that is automatically applied, and the passing of which is required for integration in git). Git diffs would regularly get very complicated, whenever a function is renamed, or if the caller-callee relations change.
author: petercordia

text:
I use ruff as my python linter and formatter and it doesnt do anything in this direction and it does not have a plugin system as far as I know and I did not like how ssort works because I wanter topdown or callers first ordering.
Currently cycles are handled by condensation and get simply the same rank and are ordered accordingly by the following sort keys if there is a tie.
The --fix option is actually just intended to reorder the definitions between themselves and you’re supposed to review after, its just a convenience flag to fix the expected order because obviously there is no way to guarantee correct code after reordering
author: Winipedia

text:
Thanks, these are helpful points!
Classes/dataclasses first is a reasonable preference. Currently, customization requires a plugin, so making preferences like that easier to configure is worth considering.
Your cycle-block suggestion makes sense too. Pyorder currently gives cycle members the same graph rank and applies the remaining sorting rules, but it doesn’t guarantee they stay together as a block.
The Git diff concern is a real trade-off. Renaming a function or changing its references can move otherwise unchanged code, making reviews and merges harder. Preserving source text doesn’t prevent that churn. I can see why you’d prefer using it occasionally rather than enforcing it on every commit.
And I agree: caller-before-callee is a convention, not an objectively correct order—the goal is predictability and if caller before callees is not a wanted goal the ssort is probably the better tool for this anyway
author: Winipedia

text:
Winipedia:

callers before callees


Really? I’d consider this to be backwards, unless I’m misunderstanding you. I generally expect to define before use, for example:
def auth():
    """Authenticate with Google. Must be done prior to any other commands."""
    ...

def list():
    """List calendars available to your account"""
    auth()
    ...

def show(calendar=DEFAULT_CALENDAR, days=3, tz=False):
    auth()
    ...

So whenever you’re looking at a symbol, the first instance of that symbol should usually be the definition of it. It’s generally easier to read that way.

author: tjreedy

text:
Linters like this exist for some other languages. For example, Rust’s clippy has module-item-order-groupings and module-items-ordered-within-groupings, which provides enough flexibility in configuration the order of items in modules/enums/traits/impls for most cases.
I don’t really care for auto-fixing myself, as a lint in my IDE would be enough. You say you’re not supporting linting suppression directives, which is unfortunate IMO, because I would definitely avoid any blanket re-ordering rules for the following levels:

Methods in classes (the method order is very subjective)
Enums (enum member order has observable runtime effects, such as when iterating, or when declaring values with enum.auto(), and it’s not syntactically possible to distinguish between an enum and a standard class). There’s the @enum.member decorator which can be applied to function definitions to turn them into a member, which will trigger your linter.

Winipedia:

Also a valid point, for me it would be not a preferable design choice that the order in which functions and classes are defined is relevant for their correctness, but thats up to the programmer oc and then you definitely should not use it.


It’s not just about whether it’s relevant to the runnability of the program. It’s about whether the order of functions is a design choice by the programmer (eg grouping related helpers together), or if it’s an irrelevant thing that you can arbitrarily destroy.
You can easily write a program that goes through your Python code and replaces all variable names with unique names guaranteed not to cause confusion. But I think most of us would rightly push back, because we know that variable names are deliberate choices that should be maintained. [1] The entire premise of pyorder is that the order of functions is not a design choice and therefore can be thrown away. I disagree, as does Terry.


There is a use-case for minification, of course, but at that point, it’s not source code any more - it’s a form of compiled binary that just so happens to be in the same language as the original. ↩︎

author: Winipedia

text:
callers-before-callees: a definition that uses another definition should be defined before it. (Hard dependencies that are needed at definition time are ordered before it, e.g. base classes, arg/kwargs defaults, or decorators).
functions-before-classes: functions should be defined before classes within the module.
visibility-ordering: public before private definitions (e.g., public, _private, __more_private)
alphabetical-ordering: definitions are ordered alphabetically.

author: Paddy3118

text:
Hi, thanks for the feedback. Mutual recursion is actually handled through graph condensation and both definitions get the same rank, which leaves the following ranks to decide order.
For functions before classes: This is simply a choice I researched and it seems to be most common. If a function is used by a class or a method of that class then it will be ordered below/after it tho and not before as the reference rank decides before this second rank.
Alphabetical was simply the final choice for the final ordering decision. Also in my experience the “When I thought of it” component loses meaning over time as the reasons for are forgotten and then later when you or someone else reads the code again, the ordering reasons at that time are less important than an objective order that is reasonable for most. This applies to most of the rules actually or at least my reasoning for writing this tool at all, as personal ordering choices lose meaning over time, especially when working with others, so an objective forced order helps maintainability a lot, I believe. But the beauty of programming is that no has to use the tool at all if they disagree, although in this case there is a plugin system so you could in fact adjust any ordering policies, remove some or add new ones as you please.
Thanks for taking the time to look at my tool, hope I could explain a bit better, I would be thrilled if you would consider running it on a few files and let me know if it us usable for someone who did not write it himself
author: Winipedia

text:
Winipedia:

I simply wrote it because I got tired of maintaining that order in my code over time and thought I wanted a tool that sorts functions and classes just like ruff sorts imports, so that my code stays organized and high in quality over time


This is something that I see very very frequently. An inexperienced programmer starts to recognize a problem (in this case, disorganized code), discovers one potential solution (automatic ordering), and believes that it will solve the problem. Fun fact: It won’t. Tools like black[1] have existed for a long time, and they haven’t solved the problem of disorganized code.
My recommendation? Don’t try to automate away creative decisions. Sure, you might get some “felt benefit” (if that’s a term) in the short term, but it won’t actually help you to make larger projects more manageable. Instead, let the code be what it wants to be. You’re a gardener, not a bulldozer.  Yes, sometimes your code will be messy. Sometimes you will have a commit where you do nothing but reorder some things because thisi s a better way to lay them out. That’s fine. By handing that control to an automated tool, you deprive yourself the opportunity to do it better - or perhaps worse, you spend all your time wrestling with the tool, thinking “THIS time it’ll be perfect and my code will be beautiful”. It won’t. Beauty can’t be condensed down to a set of rules; it’s a design decision (or rather, a constant stream of design decisions) that you, the programmer, will be making.
And if you look back on your code from a few years ago and decry it as ugly, what that really means is that you’re a better programmer now than you were. Maybe change some of that code as you make other edits. Or maybe don’t. Either is fine. Your code is your code; this is your garden, your orchard. Being “perfect” (for any definition of perfect) is unattainable; what you want is something that’s good, and productive.

text:
I’m working in a code base where sometimes there is a reason for the ordering of functions, and sometimes there isn’t. Recently one class had all their methods ordered alphabetically, and that was a big improvement for that class.
But in the code base as a whole I wouldn’t want automatic ordering of classes and functions either.
Comparison with Black is cute to me, because Black also sometimes discards the intent of the author.
Sometimes there is a good reason to prefer
def f(...): return ...

over
def f(...):
  return ...

Sometimes Black makes it impossible to put the line breaks in the most logical place (in long expressions with brackets particularly).
Yet these downsides of reduced expressiveness are generally weighed less than the advantage of regularity, and of not having the formatting of an expression depend on which author last touched it.

text:
Winipedia:

for me it would be not a preferable design choice that the order in which functions and classes are defined is relevant for their correctness,


It it not that the order has any meaning to Python, but to human readers, where the logical ordering of methods at the same call level may not be alphabetical, or where related methods are grouped with comments.



 Winipedia:

just like ruff sorts imports


Another example where one size does not fit all.  In idlelib modules (about 70), where only stdlib imports are allowed, I (and others at the time) settled on an order that makes sense for idlelib: ‘other’ stdlib modules alphabetically, tkinter and maybe tkinter submodules, other idlelib modules.
Additional notes to consider:


‘caller-first’ is also called ‘top-down’; a legitimate alternative is ‘callee-first’ or ‘bottom-up’.  If I adopted either, I would want to be able to check if my ordering was consistent with it without alphabetical checks.


Some module functions call class methods, others are called by class methods.  The appropriate function-class order, according to caller-callee rule, would then depend on the type of function.  Your function-class rule is not always consistent with your caller-callee rule.


Some code checkers are flexible, like linters that allow users to choose which rules to apply.  Some are opinionated, like Black, limiting their user base to people who agree with the choices.  Your program appears to be of the latter type, but your opening message says that you are flexible about which rules to (inflexibly?) apply.  You need to decide and be clear about your end goal.
author: tjreedy

text:
The alphabetical ordering is just a final tie breaker in the sorting key if all previous ranks are equal, but its valid to say the existing order should be preferred in a tie break, a plugin could solve this very easily.
In case it is not clear: The sorting is applied through a sorting key where each rule is a key of that larger sorting key, meaning a rule only ever decides a tiebreak after the previous rule: So callers-first is the first rule and if the order of two definitions is not decided by that then the functions-before-classes rule decides and so on, therefore rules cannot interfere with each other by design and the sorting is always consistent and reliable.
You are right, Pyorder is very inflexible if you consider the adjustablity through a config file or suppression comments which by design I did not allow. However it is very flexible via plugins, which offer perfect adjustability, it is possible to add, remove or adjust any rules in whatever way please the developer this way. The goal is to define the rules one wants their code ordered by and if they dont agree with the (admittedly strict) defaults. This way a project is able to have a constant ordering that pleases any developer who want it.
